blocks.text: 1. Real-Time Updates
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448059628-498799108.png

Observability closed by weighing its own real infrastructure cost against the debugging speed it buys. Real-Time Updates, keeping a RAG system's knowledge base current as source documents change, shifts this module's focus from operating the pipeline to keeping its underlying data actually fresh.
It detects a change in a source document and reflects it in retrieval, without a full rebuild.
2. Batch Rebuilds Versus Continuous Updates
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448059629-166003417.png
A full batch rebuild re-embeds and re-indexes every document from scratch.
Real-time updates instead apply just the specific change as soon as it happens.

blocks.text: 3. Why Staleness Is Worse In Some Domains
A fast moving domain, like live pricing or inventory, turns a stale index into actively wrong answers quickly.
How fast facts change determines how urgently updates actually need to propagate.
4. Detecting That A Source Document Changed

blocks.alt: Detecting That A Source Document Changed
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060257-270250090.png
As with extraction confidence scores in Entity Extraction, a change detection mechanism must notice an edit before any update can even begin.
A missed change means the index keeps serving the old version indefinitely.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A source document edited but never flagged to the ingestion pipeline, keeps its old, outdated chunks in the index forever, since real-time updates only apply to changes the system actually detects.
blocks.text: A source document edited but never flagged to the ingestion pipeline keeps its old, outdated chunks in the index forever, since real-time updates only apply to changes the system actually detects.
5. Updating Just The Changed Chunks, Not The Entire Document

blocks.alt: Updating Just The Changed Chunks, Not The Entire Document
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060258-194619819.png
A single edited paragraph only invalidates the specific chunks it actually touched.
Re-embedding only those changed chunks avoids the cost of reprocessing the whole document.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Update scope","Cost"],"rows":[["Whole document re-embedded","Full reprocessing cost for one small edit"],["Only changed chunks re-embedded","Minimal cost proportional to the actual edit"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Consistency Between Old And New During The Update Window

blocks.alt: Consistency Between Old And New During The Update Window
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060258-742788290.png
As with conflicting triples need a resolution rule in Graph Construction, a query arriving mid-update could retrieve a mix of stale and fresh chunks.
A real-time update pipeline needs a defined behavior for that brief inconsistent window.
7. Real-Time Updates Add Ongoing Operational Load

blocks.alt: Real-Time Updates Add Ongoing Operational Load
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060258-58940351.png
A continuously running update pipeline consumes compute even when no one is actively querying.
A real, ongoing operational cost distinct from the one-time cost of an initial batch build.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: An update pipeline watching for source changes around the clock, runs and consumes resources continuously, unlike a batch rebuild that only costs compute when it is explicitly triggered.
blocks.text: An update pipeline watching for source changes around the clock runs and consumes resources continuously, unlike a batch rebuild that only costs compute when it is explicitly triggered.
8. Eventual Consistency Is Often Acceptable
A short delay between a source change and its reflection in retrieval is often acceptable.
True instant consistency is rarely worth its added engineering cost.
9. Recognizing When Real-Time Updates Earn Their Operational Cost

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Real-Time Updates Earn Their Operational Cost
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060258-408835632.png
A fast changing knowledge base needs real-time updates.
A mostly static knowledge base is well served by periodic batch rebuilds instead.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Running a full batch rebuild for every small edit instead of updating only affected chunks.
Missing a change detection step, leaving the index silently stale indefinitely.
Ignoring the brief inconsistent window where queries could hit a mix of stale and fresh chunks.
Building a real-time update pipeline for a knowledge base that changes rarely.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Real-time updates keep a RAG system's knowledge base current as source documents change.
A batch rebuild reprocesses everything; real-time updates apply just the specific change.
Fast moving domains turn a stale index into actively wrong answers quickly.
A change detection mechanism must notice an edit before any update can begin.
Only the specific chunks an edit touched need re-embedding, not the whole document.
A real-time pipeline needs defined behavior for the brief window where old and new data mix.
A continuously running update pipeline consumes compute even with no active queries, a real ongoing cost.
A short delay before a change is reflected is often acceptable; instant consistency rarely justifies its cost.
